01-quantum-models: A quantum model is a hypothesis class fixed by an encoding, a parameterised circuit, and a measurement.
Expressivity, trainability, and generalisation need different evidence; none of them alone is an advantage.
An advantage claim is a conditional with a task, a baseline, a budget, and a quantifier order.
02-data-encoding: Basis, amplitude, and angle encodings trade qubit count against preparation cost and preserved geometry.
Amplitude encoding discards the norm, and angle encoding is periodic, so both can be non-injective on real data.
The encoding fixes the kernel; a product-state angle encoding gives a classical kernel exactly.
03-kernels: The representer theorem reduces a kernel method to linear algebra on the Gram matrix.
One kernel entry is one circuit run; the shot cost grows as 1/K, so small entries are expensive.
Concentration drives entries to 1/2^n with comparable spread, making the matrix uninformative.
04-variational: A variational model is four decisions: encoding, ansatz, readout, and training rule; only the second is usually called the ansatz.
Measurement cost is settings times shots, and precision scales as 1/epsilon^2, so each decimal digit is a hundredfold increase.
Shallow depth bounds entanglement across a cut, and how the measured terms are combined decides whether gradients survive.
